title: Flow
summary: Cold and hot Flows, StateFlow, SharedFlow, operators and lifecycle-aware collection.

lesson.heading: Cold Flows
lesson.body:
A `Flow` is an asynchronous stream of values built on coroutines. It's **cold**: the `flow { }` block does nothing until someone calls `collect`, and every collector reruns the producer from scratch.

`collect` is a suspend function, so collection respects structured concurrency: if the scope is cancelled, collection stops.

lesson.heading: Operators
lesson.body:
Intermediate operators (`map`, `filter`, `onEach`, `distinctUntilChanged`, `debounce`) return new Flows without running anything. `combine` merges the latest value of several flows, `zip` pairs them one to one, and `flatMapLatest` cancels the previous inner flow on every new value (perfect for search).

`flowOn` changes the context of the **upstream** operators, while the collector stays in its own context. `catch` intercepts upstream exceptions.

lesson.heading: StateFlow
lesson.body:
`StateFlow` is a **hot** flow that always holds a current value (`value`) and requires an initial one. New collectors immediately receive the latest state.

It's **conflated** and ignores equal assignments (compared with `equals`), which makes it ideal for UI state. In the ViewModel you expose a read-only `StateFlow` and update the private `MutableStateFlow` with `update { }`, which is atomic.

lesson.heading: SharedFlow and stateIn
lesson.body:
`SharedFlow` is hot, has no initial value, and is configurable with `replay` and `extraBufferCapacity`: you use it to broadcast events to multiple collectors. A `StateFlow` is effectively a SharedFlow with replay 1 and distinctUntilChanged.

To turn a cold flow into a hot one, use `stateIn` or `shareIn`. The recommended pattern is `stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial)`: the upstream stops 5 seconds after the last collector leaves, so it survives rotation without wasting resources in the background.
lesson.code:
val uiState: StateFlow<List<Item>> = repo.items()
    .map { it.sortedBy(Item::name) }
    .stateIn(
        viewModelScope,
        SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000),
        emptyList()
    )

lesson.heading: Collecting on Android, and LiveData
lesson.body:
In Compose, use `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()`, which stops collecting when the lifecycle drops below `STARTED`. With Views, use `repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED)` inside `lifecycleScope.launch`; `launchWhenStarted` is deprecated.

`LiveData` is lifecycle-aware on its own, doesn't require an initial value, and re-emits equal values too, but it has few operators and is tied to Android. StateFlow is pure Kotlin, testable without a framework, and rich in operators: today it's the default choice.

lesson.heading: In the interview
lesson.body:
Typical question: **"What's the difference between Flow, StateFlow and SharedFlow?"**. Short answer: Flow is cold and runs the producer for each collector; StateFlow is hot, always has a value, and is meant for state; SharedFlow is hot, has no initial value and a configurable replay, and suits events.

Mention `stateIn` with `WhileSubscribed(5_000)`, lifecycle-aware collection, and why StateFlow has replaced LiveData in new codebases.

questions.explanation: The Flow is cold: the block runs from scratch for each collector, not at creation.
whyWrong: A Flow is cold: `flow { }` only defines the block, which runs when someone calls `collect`.
There's no caching: every `collect` reruns the block from scratch, so "start" is printed each time.
It does get printed, but only when the flow is collected: every `collect` runs the block.

questions.prompt: What happens when you assign a `MutableStateFlow` a value equal (equals) to the current one?
options: No emission: equal values are ignored
The value is queued in the buffer
questions.explanation: StateFlow applies an equals-based distinctUntilChanged: collectors receive nothing. LiveData, on the other hand, would re-emit.
whyWrong: That's how LiveData behaves; StateFlow compares with `equals` and doesn't emit if the value hasn't changed.
Assigning an equal value is perfectly legal: it simply produces no emission.
StateFlow has no buffer of values: it only keeps the current value, and an equal one is discarded.

questions.prompt: Which one requires an initial value?
questions.explanation: StateFlow always has a `value`, so it must be initialized; MutableSharedFlow() has no initial value.
whyWrong: `MutableSharedFlow()` is created without an initial value: it may never have emitted anything.
Only StateFlow always has a `value` and therefore requires an initial one; SharedFlow doesn't.
StateFlow can't exist without a value: `MutableStateFlow(initial)` requires it right in the constructor.

questions.prompt: Which part of the chain does `flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)` affect?
questions.explanation: flowOn only changes the upstream context; collect stays in the context of the calling coroutine.
whyWrong: It's the opposite: `flowOn` affects the operators that come before it (upstream), not the ones after it.
The collector stays in the context of the coroutine that calls `collect`: `flowOn` doesn't move it, which is what context preservation guarantees.
`flowOn` doesn't change the whole chain: it only touches the upstream, up to any previous `flowOn`.

options: It keeps the upstream alive 5 s after the last collector (rotation)
It delays the first emission by 5 seconds
It's the timeout for the first value
questions.explanation: A rotation takes less than 5 s, so the upstream doesn't restart; if the app stays in the background longer, it stops and saves resources.
whyWrong: The parameter isn't an initial delay: it's `stopTimeoutMillis`, i.e. how long to wait after the last subscriber before stopping the upstream.
There's no timeout on the first value: `stateIn` already has an initial value, and the 5000 ms say when to stop the upstream with no subscribers.
No replay is configured here: `stateIn` produces a StateFlow that only keeps the latest value, and 5_000 is in milliseconds.

options: It stops collecting below the STARTED state
It converts the Flow to LiveData
questions.explanation: It respects the lifecycle: when the app is in the background it stops collecting, avoiding wasted work.
whyWrong: It's not about speed: the difference is that it stops collecting when the lifecycle drops below `STARTED`.
It works with Flows, not LiveData: for LiveData there's `observeAsState`.
It doesn't convert anything to LiveData: it returns a Compose `State<T>`, collecting only while the lifecycle is at least `STARTED`.

questions.explanation: map produces 10, 20, 30; filter keeps those greater than 10. `toList()` is a suspending terminal operator.
whyWrong: That's the result of `map` alone: then `filter { it > 10 }` drops the 10.
The filter works on the values already multiplied by 10, not the originals: 20 and 30 remain.
The filter is `> 10`, not `> 20`: 20 passes and stays in the list.

questions.prompt: For a search that must cancel the previous request on every new input, which operator do you use?
questions.explanation: flatMapLatest cancels the previous inner flow as soon as a new value arrives; concat and merge run them all to completion.
whyWrong: `flatMapConcat` waits for each inner flow to finish before moving to the next: old searches aren't cancelled.
`flatMapMerge` runs the inner flows concurrently without cancelling them: stale results could arrive after newer ones.
`zip` pairs up the elements of two flows: it doesn't turn each input into a request or cancel the previous ones.

questions.prompt: What does a new collector receive immediately?
questions.code:
val shared = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(replay = 1)
shared.emit(1)
shared.emit(2)
// new collector
questions.explanation: With replay = 1 the cache keeps only the last emitted value, which is replayed to new collectors.
whyWrong: Without replay the new collector would receive nothing, but here `replay = 1` keeps the last value for late subscribers.
The replay cache holds a single element: when 2 arrives, 1 is dropped.
The cache keeps the latest value, not the first: after `emit(2)`, 1 has been replaced.

questions.prompt: Which difference between LiveData and StateFlow is correct?
options: LiveData is cold, StateFlow is hot
StateFlow is lifecycle-aware on its own
StateFlow requires an initial value, LiveData doesn't
questions.explanation: StateFlow must be initialized and ignores duplicates; LiveData is lifecycle-aware but re-emits equal values. For StateFlow, lifecycle awareness has to be added at collection time.
whyWrong: Both are hot: LiveData holds the current value and notifies observers, without rerunning anything for each one.
It's LiveData that is lifecycle-aware: for StateFlow, awareness is added at collection time with `repeatOnLifecycle` or `collectAsStateWithLifecycle`.
It's StateFlow that ignores equal values; LiveData re-emits even a value identical to the current one.
